<p class="sardine-eyebrow">DERAILED / MARINE LIFE / AN AQUARIUM DETOUR</p>

# Who is leading the sardines?

<p class="sardine-lede">A ray appeared. The sardines scattered. My aunt had a theory. I had a question.</p>

## 01 / The moment behind the glass

I was visiting **Aquamarine Fukushima** with my relatives when I stopped to watch the Japanese sardines. I love how fish swim together. So many silver bodies changing direction, apparently without bumping into one another.

Then a large ray—an *エイ*—came into view. The sardines scattered around it so effortlessly that the movement looked almost choreographed.

My aunt watched the same scene and offered a wonderfully natural explanation:

<blockquote class="story-quote">
  <p>“There must be a good leader.”</p>
  <footer>— My aunt, watching the sardines</footer>
</blockquote>

Of course! When a group moves that beautifully, it's tempting to imagine someone giving excellent directions.

But how would the others know when to turn? Could one fish possibly tell hundreds of fish where to go?

And what if **there was no leader at all?**

## 02 / Let's build a very small ocean

I couldn't bring the aquarium home. But I could draw one sardine, give it a movement engine, make 47 more, and see what happens when they start paying attention to their neighbours.

This is a little simulation, not a replica of the aquarium. There is no secret captain hidden among the fish.

<div class="sardine-intro">ONE FISH → MANY FISH → NEIGHBOURS → A SCHOOL?</div>

## 03 / An experiment for my aunt

The tank starts with a school of small sardines. They look similar, but each has its own position, direction, size variation, and tail rhythm.

Try the experiment in this order:

1. **Watch the school.** Is it obvious which fish is in charge? (Hint: none has been designated as the leader.)
2. **Switch to Independent.** The fish keep swimming, but they no longer react to one another. Does the tank still look like a single group?
3. **Switch back to Schooling.** The same fish now respond to nearby neighbours. Watch the paths change; no one receives a group-wide command.
4. **Remove a rule.** Turn one of the three schooling sliders down to zero. What changes when the fish stop trying to align, stay together, or keep their distance?

You can change the number of fish from **1 to 120**, or shrink them to make room for a denser crowd. For a different experiment, tap the tank to give everyone a **shared destination**. That is an external cue, not a leader fish—so use **Free swim** when you want to study coordination without a common goal.

## 04 / Three tiny instructions

The simulator borrows an idea from **Boids**, a computational model published by Craig Reynolds in 1987. Instead of scripting an impressive formation for the whole group, we give each individual a few local rules:

- **Separation:** don't get too close to the neighbours right beside you.
- **Alignment:** turn roughly the way your nearby neighbours are facing.
- **Cohesion:** stay near your neighbourhood instead of wandering away.

Each sardine calculates its own next move from the fish nearby. The simulator computes those suggestions from the same instant before anyone moves. There is no instruction saying, *“Form a beautiful school now.”*

When a pattern emerges from many small interactions, we call that **emergence**.

The surprising part isn't that the fish follow rules. It's that **none of the rules describes the whole school**.

## 05 / But what about the ray?

That's the part of the aquarium moment this little tank **doesn't simulate yet**.

The ray caught our attention because the sardines suddenly made space around it. Our current model can explore coordination among neighbours, but it has no ray, no changing threat, and none of the sensory complexity of real fish. It cannot tell us exactly why the sardines moved as they did that day.

That makes the next detour rather irresistible: *What if a ray moved through the simulated school?* Would local avoidance rules be enough for the fish to scatter around it—without anyone giving an order?

My aunt's explanation might still have seemed right to an observer. But a school can look coordinated even when no individual is coordinating it.

<p class="sardine-outro">“There must be a good leader.”<br>Or perhaps there doesn't have to be one.</p>

<p class="sardine-source">**Seen:** a school of sardines and a ray, on a family visit to Aquamarine Fukushima. **Model:** a simplified two-dimensional interpretation of Craig Reynolds' <a href="https://www.red3d.com/cwr/papers/1987/boids.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">1987 Boids paper</a>, not a biological explanation of that specific encounter. <a href="https://github.com/chichacha/derailed/issues/16">DERAILED #16</a> · <a href="https://github.com/chichacha/psychic-pento-guacamole/issues/115">Gomasu #115</a>.</p>
